analysis.one_liner: Bans big meatpackers from owning, feeding, or controlling the livestock they slaughter.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it was sent to the House Agriculture Committee on March 28, 2012, then to a livestock subcommittee on April 12, and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would revive a long-standing prohibition against meatpacking companies owning, feeding, or controlling the cattle, hogs, or other livestock they slaughter, unless the farmer running the operation still manages it day to day. A few narrow exceptions apply: animals bought within a week of slaughter, farmer-owned cooperatives, small packers that do not have to report daily prices, and packers that own only one processing plant. Large packers that already own livestock would have up to 18 months (for hog packers) to unwind those arrangements. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent livestock farmers and ranchers. When a packer owns or controls the animals it slaughters, it needs fewer cattle and hogs from the open market, which shrinks the number of buyers independent producers can sell to and pushes down the prices they receive. Blocking that 'captive supply' would restore a bigger, more competitive market for animals sold by independent farms, and rural communities where that money is spent would benefit as well. Farmer-owned cooperatives are explicitly protected by an exception in the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a packer from owning, feeding, or controlling livestock through any arrangement that strips the producer of real management control over the farming operation.

Exempts farmer-owned cooperatives whose members own and deliver the livestock themselves, along with single-plant packers and packers not required to report daily price and quantity information, so the ban targets large integrated packers rather than smaller or grower-owned slaughter operations.
Gives existing packers a transition period — 18 months for hog packers and up to 180 days for other livestock — so they can unwind integrated feeding arrangements rather than shut down abruptly.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies that own feeding operations or hold production contracts giving them control over livestock, and large integrated livestock-feeding enterprises tied to them. If packers must buy more animals on the open market, their sourcing costs could rise, which they argue could translate into higher meat prices at the grocery store.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large meatpacking companies and feeding operations

drawbacks.text: The bill carries substantial carve-outs: animals bought within seven days of slaughter, farmer-owned cooperatives, packers exempt from daily price reporting, and single-plant packers are all excepted, which limits how much of the packer-livestock structure it actually unwinds.

A good-faith objection packers raise: vertical integration lets them guarantee animal supply, quality, and food-safety standards efficiently, and ending it could raise their costs — costs that may partly show up in retail meat prices for consumers.

The effectiveness of the ban depends on enforcement against indirect arrangements; the bill's definition of control ('operational, managerial, or supervisory control') would require the Agriculture Department to police contract terms that packers could otherwise redesign to stay just outside the line.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a more open market where independent farmers have more buyers and better price competition — is real and directly aimed at a market structure that independent producer groups have fought for decades. The costs fall mainly on the packers, though consumers could see some of the added sourcing cost in meat prices, and the carve-outs plus enforcement challenges make the bill a partial fix rather than a full one. On balance the bill is modest, targeted, and honestly weighted toward producers over packers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, then to its livestock subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bruce Braley of Iowa introduced the bill on March 28, 2012.
The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced.
On April 12, 2012, it was referred to the subcommittee handling livestock, dairy, and poultry — a stage most bills never leave.
No further action appears in the record, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, so the bill expired with no vote in either chamber.

The bill would have amended the Packers and Stockyards Act of 1921, a law meant to keep livestock markets fair, by barring packers from owning or controlling slaughter livestock when the producer no longer materially manages the operation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies that own or control livestock through feeding operations and contracts kept that market structure intact, and independent livestock producers gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Bruce Braley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought a change to the Packers and Stockyards Act limiting packer ownership of livestock.

for.name: A House Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional supporter on the record.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor consideration of the bill, leaving it to die in subcommittee referral.

against.name: Large meatpacking companies
against.role: Packer industry (major cattle and hog processors)
against.what_they_did: Long opposed packer-ownership bans like this one, arguing vertical integration lowers their costs and benefits consumers; the bill received no committee action that would threaten them.

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Democrats supported the bill on the record and no one voted on it, so the record shows too little to read a partisan pattern either way.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from owning, feeding, or controlling the livestock they slaughter, forcing them to buy more animals from independent producers on the open market. Their gain from keeping captive supply comes at the cost of lower prices and thinner markets for independent farmers.

industries.industry: Independent livestock producers (cattle, hog, and sheep farms)
industries.note: With packers barred from controlling livestock, independent farmers would have more buyers competing for their animals, supporting better prices and the rural economies that depend on them.
The bill exempts cooperatives whose active members own and deliver the livestock for slaughter, preserving this producer-owned channel for getting animals to market.
